lead: A belt wrapped round a pulley can carry a large tight-side tension and a much smaller slack-side tension because friction acts along the whole curved contact. The ratio of these tensions grows exponentially with the coefficient of friction and the angle of contact. A V-belt sits in a groove, so the same friction produces a larger ratio. This is why V-belts drive machines, why a rope round a bollard holds a boat, and why a capstan lets one person hold a ship. The next sections derive both ratios and apply them.
prereq: You need: the laws of dry friction and the coefficient μ from Chapter 3.4.

blocks.text: Take a small piece of belt in contact with the pulley over a small angle dθ. Let T be the tension at one end of the piece and T + dT at the other. The tension rises toward the tight side, so dT is positive in the direction in which the belt tends to slip. The pulley pushes outward on the piece with normal force dN. Friction μ dN acts along the pulley surface and opposes that slip.

Resolve forces on the piece. In the radial direction, the two tension forces have inward components that balance dN: dN = T dθ. The term dT dθ/2 is second order and is dropped. In the tangential direction, friction balances the tension change: μ dN = dT.
Combine: μ T dθ = dT, so dT/T = μ dθ. Integrate from the slack side to the tight side. The left side gives ln(T_tight/T_slack); the right side gives μθ.

blocks.where: T_tight is the tight-side tension in N; T_slack is the slack-side tension in N; μ is the coefficient of friction, a pure number; θ is the total angle of contact in radians; e = 2.718... is the base of natural logarithms.

blocks.text: This is the limiting (maximum) ratio, reached only when the belt is on the point of slipping. A belt carrying less than its limiting torque has T<sub>tight</sub>/T<sub>slack</sub> smaller than e<sup>μθ</sup>. The worked example below assumes the belt is just about to slip.

The ratio is exponential because every small arc adds friction proportional to the local tension. A larger tension creates a larger friction force, which supports a still larger tension difference. θ is the total wrap angle, not the angle of one small element. A 120° contact is 2.094 rad, not 120.

A V-belt has a trapezium section. It runs in a pulley groove with total angle 2β, so β is the half groove angle. β is measured between one sloping face of the groove and the centre plane. The belt touches two faces, not one.

Let R be the total radial reaction needed to balance the tension forces, as dN was for the flat belt. Each face carries normal force N. The radial components of the two normals add: 2N sin β = R, so N = R/(2 sin β). Friction on both faces is 2 μ N = μ R / sin β. The friction is therefore the same as a flat belt with an effective coefficient μ/sin β.

blocks.where: β is the half groove angle in radians; 2β is the full groove angle; T_tight, T_slack, μ and θ are as defined for the flat belt.

blocks.text: For β = 20°, sin β = 0.342, so the effective coefficient is about 2.92 times μ. With μ = 0.3, the effective value is 0.877. The same μ and θ give a much larger ratio than a flat belt. This is the reason V-belts are used where a small wrap angle or a compact drive must transmit torque without slip.
Use the ratio in four steps.

items: Mark the tight side and the slack side. The ratio T<sub>tight</sub>/T<sub>slack</sub> is greater than 1; the limiting value e<sup>μθ</sup> (for a flat belt) applies only at impending slip, so a belt carrying less than its limiting torque has a smaller ratio.
Convert the contact angle to radians: θ_rad = θ_deg × π / 180.
Flat belt: substitute μ and θ. V-belt: substitute the half angle β in sin β; never use the full groove angle 2β.
Solve for the unknown tension. Check that the tight tension comes out larger than the slack tension.

blocks.text: For the example below, the belt is at impending slip, μ = 0.3 and θ = 120° = 2.094 rad. The flat-belt ratio is e<sup>0.6283</sup> = 1.874. The V-belt ratio with β = 20° is e<sup>0.6283/0.3420</sup> = e<sup>1.837</sup> = 6.279. A V-belt therefore holds a much smaller slack tension for the same tight tension.

Some syllabi call this rope friction or capstan friction. The same formula applies to a rope round a post, a bollard or a capstan. The rope does not need a groove; the capstan effect comes from the curved contact alone. Torque and power transmission belong to design courses.

figure.caption: Tension ratio against contact angle for μ = 0.3. The V-belt curve uses half angle β = 20° and rises much faster than the flat-belt curve.

spec.aria: A plot of tight-to-slack tension ratio against contact angle for a flat belt and a V-belt with half angle 20 degrees.

examples.question: A flat belt on a pulley has μ = 0.3, angle of contact 120°, and tight tension 500 N. Assume the belt is on the point of slipping. Find the slack tension. Repeat for a V-belt in a 40° groove, taking half angle β = 20°.
steps: Convert the contact angle: θ = 120° × π / 180 = 2.094 rad.
Flat belt exponent: μθ = 0.3 × 2.094 = 0.6283. Then e<sup>0.6283</sup> = 1.874.
V-belt half angle β = 20°, so sin β = sin 20° = 0.3420. The exponent is μθ / sin β = 0.6283 / 0.3420 = 1.837.
Then e<sup>1.837</sup> = 6.279. V-belt slack tension: T_slack = 500 / 6.279 = 79.6 N.
Check: both slack tensions are less than the tight tension, as they must be. The V-belt gives the smaller slack tension for the same tight tension.
examples.answer: The flat-belt slack tension is 266.8 N (about 267 N), and the V-belt slack tension is 79.6 N.
examples.check:
import math
mu=0.3
theta=math.radians(120)
T1=500.0
T2_flat=T1/math.exp(mu*theta)
beta=math.radians(20)
T2_v=T1/math.exp(mu*theta/math.sin(beta))
print(round(T2_flat,1))
print(round(T2_v,1))

traps: Putting θ in degrees. A 120° contact must enter the formula as 2.094 rad.
Using the full groove angle 2β instead of the half angle β. For a 40° groove, β = 20°.
Inverting the ratio. T_tight/T_slack is greater than 1; a result below 1 means the sides were swapped.
Check the calculator's angle mode. sin 20° = 0.342 and sin 40° = 0.643; entering the full groove angle or leaving the calculator in radian mode both give a wrong exponent.
Forgetting that θ is the actual wrap angle. It is not always 180° or 360°; a small pulley or a crossed belt changes it.

quiz.q: State the flat-belt tension ratio and define each symbol.
quiz.a: T<sub>tight</sub>/T<sub>slack</sub> = e<sup>μθ</sup> at impending slip; μ is the coefficient of friction and θ is the total angle of contact in radians.

quiz.q: What is the angle of contact of a belt?
quiz.a: The total angle, measured at the pulley centre, over which the belt touches the pulley. It must be used in radians in the belt-friction formula.

quiz.q: Why does the tension ratio come out exponential rather than linear?
quiz.a: On a small arc, the friction force is μ dN and dN is proportional to the local tension T. Thus dT/T = μ dθ. Integrating adds equal fractional tension changes over equal angular increments, which gives an exponential.

quiz.q: Why does a V-belt give a larger tension ratio than a flat belt for the same μ and θ?
quiz.a: The groove has two contact faces. The normal reactions on the faces have radial components, so the total normal force is larger for the same radial reaction. The effective coefficient is μ/sin β, which is larger than μ because sin β is less than 1.

quiz.q: A flat belt has μ = 0.25, angle of contact 150°, and tight tension 800 N. Find the slack tension.
A V-belt has the same μ = 0.25 and θ = 150°, and a groove half angle β = 18°. The tight tension is 800 N. Find the slack tension.
For a flat belt, if μ is doubled while θ stays the same, how does T_tight/T_slack change?
quiz.a: It becomes e<sup>2μθ</sup> = (e<sup>μθ</sup>)², so the old ratio is squared. Doubling μ does not double the ratio; it squares it.

quiz.q: A flat belt and a V-belt have the same tight tension, μ and θ. Which has the lower slack tension, and why?
quiz.a: The V-belt has the lower slack tension. Its groove increases the normal reaction for the same radial force, so the effective coefficient is μ/sin β, which is larger than μ. The ratio T<sub>tight</sub>/T<sub>slack</sub> is therefore larger, and T<sub>slack</sub> = T<sub>tight</sub> divided by that larger ratio is smaller.

beyond: Not for the exam. V-ribbed belts work by friction and give a large effective friction ratio with small slip. Toothed or timing belts are different: they transmit torque by teeth meshing with the pulley grooves, so they cannot slip and no friction ratio applies to them. The capstan equation also appears in textile yarn tension control, cable laying and climbing-rope belay devices. Search for capstan equation, V-belt effective friction and belt drive slip. Modern design courses add centrifugal tension and belt mass, which the simple ratio here ignores.
